claims.text: The starting material is an as-cast, AlCoCrFeNi-like eutectic high-entropy alloy with hierarchical dual-phase lamellar colonies.
Approximately 0.5 at% boron is introduced during alloy casting.
The boron addition is followed by a 10–20 minute rapid solution treatment at approximately 0.9 times the melting temperature of the softer phase and rapid quenching.
The proposed processing will cause controlled boron segregation at lamellar interphase boundaries.
The treatment can avoid the formation of brittle boride phases if its parameters are optimized.
Boron-enriched interfaces will have modified chemistry and enhanced boundary cohesion.
Boron segregation lowers the local boundary energy and modifies interfacial bonding.
The chemically modified interfaces will act as active sites for earlier and more uniform dislocation nucleation and emission.
Enhanced dislocation emission from interfaces will alleviate dislocation pile-ups and reduce associated local stress concentrations.
Improved interface cohesion and reduced stress concentration will delay microcrack initiation and propagation.
The untreated alloy typically has limited room-temperature ductility because dislocation pile-ups at phase boundaries produce stress concentrations and microcracking.
The treatment will significantly increase room-temperature tensile elongation relative to the untreated alloy.
The treatment will maintain or modestly increase the strength of the untreated dual-phase lamellar alloy.
The proposed property improvement applies to room-temperature, quasi-static tensile loading at a strain rate of about 10^-3 s^-1.
Excessive or uncontrolled boron segregation may form brittle boride phases.
The intervention's effects at other strain rates, temperatures, and long-term service conditions are not established.
